idiom_name: parallel primitive arrays (FloatArray/IntArray) with index handles and @JvmInline value classes
implementation_notes: Kotlin compiles to JVM objects, so the packed layout is written by hand exactly as in Java: parallel primitive arrays (FloatArray, IntArray) walked by index replace an Array<Particle> of heap objects. Kotlin's own lever is the inline value class: an @JvmInline value class 'must have a single property initialized in the primary constructor' and is represented by that property at runtime, so a handle or unit wrapper costs nothing - but the compiler boxes when the value is treated as another type, used as a generic argument, made nullable, or assigned into an array (kotlinlang.org lists array assignment as an allocation case), so Array<EntityId> is an array of objects. For data-oriented kernels the reliable shapes are counted indexed loops over primitive arrays and inline value classes used as parameters/locals only.
pitfalls: Inline value classes box whenever they are stored in an array, made nullable, or used as a generic/interface type, so Array<EntityId> is not a packed Int array - keep handles in IntArray on the hot path.
data class instances are heap objects with headers, and List<Float> boxes: Kotlin collections are JVM collections, so hot data belongs in primitive arrays or buffers.
Methods on inline classes are compiled to static functions with mangled names; reflection and Java interop see the underlying type, which surprises deserialization and code that inspects members.
Lambdas/sequences over arrays add indirection (and allocate unless inlined); indexed loops are the predictable choice in kernels.
